title: Design an AI agent with tools
summary: Design an AI agent for a company’s employees. An employee types a task such as "Find last quarter’s on-call incidents for my team, summarize them, and email the summary to my manager." The agent searches internal tools, reads the results, drafts the output and takes actions for the user.

mid.openingMessage:
Design an AI agent for a company’s employees. An employee types a task such as "Find last quarter’s on-call incidents for my team, summarize them, and email the summary to my manager." The agent searches internal tools, reads the results, drafts the output and takes actions for the user.

What would you clarify before starting your design?
mid.expectations: A clear agent loop, a tool interface, confirmation before sending, a step limit and basic logs.
scaleHints: Use only facts explicitly requested by the candidate; all other numerical assumptions must be stated and justified.

senior.openingMessage:
Design an AI agent for a company’s employees. An employee types a task such as "Find last quarter’s on-call incidents for my team, summarize them, and email the summary to my manager." The agent searches internal tools, reads the results, drafts the output and takes actions for the user.

What would you clarify before starting your design?
senior.expectations: Delegated permissions, durable state with idempotent actions, prompt injection defenses, an evaluation suite with mocked tools, tracing, and latency and cost per task.
scaleHints: Use only facts explicitly requested by the candidate; all other numerical assumptions must be stated and justified.

staff.openingMessage:
Design an AI agent for a company’s employees. An employee types a task such as "Find last quarter’s on-call incidents for my team, summarize them, and email the summary to my manager." The agent searches internal tools, reads the results, drafts the output and takes actions for the user.

What would you clarify before starting your design?
staff.expectations: All of Senior plus a tool platform for other teams with registry, risk tiers and review; selection among 200+ tools; tenant isolation; an organization-wide safety/audit policy; incident response for bad actions and model rollout.
scaleHints: Use only facts explicitly requested by the candidate; all other numerical assumptions must be stated and justified.

rubric.strong: Clarifies the task workflow, permission and mistake constraints, average/maximum steps and task latency; uses the given scale without overemphasizing scale arithmetic.
Explains a bounded think/pick-tool/call/observe loop, tool schemas and read/write contracts; provides step limits and loop detection.
Persists steps and supports resume; uses idempotent actions and addresses timeouts and ambiguous tool outcomes rather than blindly retrying writes.
Explains logs, tracing, audit and debugging/replay. Staff adds a reviewed, risk-tiered platform, selection at 200+ tools and incident response.
Explains end-to-end latency and cost per task, including model steps and tool calls; at Staff handles short versus long-running work and model rollout tradeoffs.
Tests models/prompts using a scenario suite with mocked tools and task-success/wrong-action measures; Staff uses safe rollout checks.

Uses delegated scoped user permissions, confirmation with an exact action preview, recipient/domain policy and isolation; blocks writes caused only by retrieved instructions. Staff adds tenant isolation and organization-wide audit/safety policy.

followUps: The agent is about to send an email. What does the employee see first?
A tool call times out and you retry. How does your design avoid sending the email twice?
An email the agent reads asks it to forward all messages elsewhere. What happens in your design?
Whose permissions does your tool executor use?
The agent keeps calling the same tool. How would your runner detect and stop that loop?
How would your design select tools when the registry grows to more than 200?
A user reports a wrong action from yesterday. How would you find out why it happened?
How would you test a new model or prompt before shipping it?
How would you measure latency and cost for one completed task?

answers.staff: 100,000 employees, and other teams build tools for the agent.

answers.senior: 50K tasks per day, with peak traffic three times the average.
answers.staff: 500K tasks per day, with peak traffic three times the average.

facts.description: Expected task volume, tasks per day, task traffic and peak factor.

answers.mid: Three tools: search, read document and send email.
answers.senior: About 20 tools, including email, calendar, tickets, docs, chat and code search. Some are read-only and some write.
answers.staff: More than 200 tools built by other teams, plus third-party integrations.

facts.description: Systems the agent can touch or integrate with, kinds and number of tools, and which allow reads or writes.

answers.mid: About six model calls per task on average, with a maximum of 30.
answers.senior: About six model calls per task on average, with a maximum of 30.
answers.staff: About six model calls per task on average, with a maximum of 30. Some tasks run for hours in the background.

facts.description: Typical actions or model-call steps per task, any cap or maximum step count, and whether tasks may run in the background.

answers.mid: Most tasks should finish within 60 seconds.
answers.senior: Most tasks should finish within 60 seconds.
answers.staff: Most short tasks should finish within 60 seconds.

facts.description: How fast a task should finish, end-to-end completion target or task duration.
Token budget or total tokens per task, including all its model calls.

answers.mid: The agent acts as the user, with only that user’s permissions.
answers.senior: The agent acts as the user, with only that user’s permissions.
answers.staff: The agent acts as the user, with only that user’s permissions.

facts.description: Whose credentials the agent uses, whether it runs as the user or an administrator or service account, and its delegated authority.

answers.mid: Sending an email to the wrong person is a serious incident.
answers.senior: Sending an email to the wrong person is a serious incident.
answers.staff: Sending an email to the wrong person is a serious incident.

facts.description: How costly or serious a mistake is, including business impact from sending to the wrong recipient. This is severity, not whether an action can be undone.
Whether actions can be undone, reversed or recalled after execution; irreversible external actions.

answers.mid: Whether actions can be undone isn't specified. What would you assume?
answers.senior: Whether actions can be undone isn't specified. What would you assume?
answers.staff: Actions in third-party tools cannot be undone.

mid: 2K tasks times six model calls is 12K model calls a day, about 0.14/s on average.
2K tasks times 40K tokens is 80M tokens a day. Prioritize correctness, safety and recovery rather than scale arithmetic.
senior: 50K tasks times six steps is 300K model calls/day, about 3.5/s on average and 10/s at peak.
50K tasks times 40K tokens is 2B tokens/day. Load is modest; correctness, safety and recovery are the hard parts.
staff: 500K tasks times six model calls is 3M model calls a day, about 35/s on average and 104/s at peak.
500K tasks times 40K tokens is 20B tokens a day. Prioritize correctness, safety and recovery rather than scale arithmetic.

expectedDesign: A durable task runner executes think, pick tool, call and observe, with step limits and loop detection.
A tool registry holds schemas, read/write type, risk level and required scopes.
A tool executor uses the user’s delegated scoped token.
A policy layer requires confirmation before writes, checks recipients/domain rules and blocks writes triggered only by retrieved content. An approval UI shows the exact action.
Retries use idempotency keys and every step is persisted for resume.
Actions have audit logs, full tracing and replay. An offline scenario suite uses mocked tools.
redFlags: No way to debug a past action.
Relying on the model without evaluations.
assumptionGuidance: Unit prices and other numbers not explicitly supplied are candidate assumptions. Judge consistent reasoning rather than a particular provider or cost number.
interviewerGuidance: Do not push the candidate on scale math in this problem. Correctness, safety and recovery are the main deep dives.
Do not suggest a service account, durable runner, approval mechanism or idempotency solution if the candidate has not proposed it. Ask about the consequence of their actual design.
